explain: Trace gcd(48, 18) in the new order, one rule at a time. Cycle 1: load gives (48, 18); subtract makes it (30, 18); swap sees 30 ≥ 18 and does nothing. Cycle 2: subtract gives (12, 18); swap sees 12 < 18 and gives (18, 12). Cycle 3: subtract gives (6, 12); swap gives (12, 6). Cycle 4: subtract gives (6, 6). Cycle 5: subtract gives (0, 6); swap gives (6, 0). At cycle 6 y is 0, so io_done is high at cycle 6, one cycle earlier than the original order (cycle 7). The result is 6 either way. On other inputs the difference can go the other way.

-open XBlue
+-- The proof above is for the original design; it does not apply to this variant.
-structure St where
-  x : BitVec 8
-  y : BitVec 8
-  busy : BitVec 1
-/-- One clock cycle of the design itself. -/
-def next (reset start : BitVec 1) (a b : BitVec 8) (s : St) : St :=
-  let r := (mkGcd.design.cycle (.cons reset (.cons start (.cons a (.cons b .nil))))
-              (.cons s.x (.cons s.y (.cons s.busy .nil)))).regs
-  ⟨r.get mkGcd.x, r.get mkGcd.y, r.get mkGcd.busy⟩
--- The five rules, each as a plain function on the registers.
-def finish (s : St) : St :=
-  let fires := s.busy = 1#1 ∧ s.y = 0#8
-  ⟨s.x, s.y, if fires then 0#1 else s.busy⟩
-def load (start : BitVec 1) (a b : BitVec 8) (s : St) : St :=
-  let fires := start = 1#1 ∧ s.busy = 0#1
-  ⟨if fires then a else s.x, if fires then b else s.y, if fires then 1#1 else s.busy⟩
-def swap (s : St) : St :=
-  let fires := s.busy = 1#1 ∧ s.x < s.y ∧ s.y ≠ 0#8
-  ⟨if fires then s.y else s.x, if fires then s.x else s.y, s.busy⟩
-def subtract (s : St) : St :=
-  let fires := s.busy = 1#1 ∧ s.y ≤ s.x ∧ s.y ≠ 0#8
-  ⟨if fires then s.x - s.y else s.x, s.y, s.busy⟩
-def clear (reset : BitVec 1) (s : St) : St :=
-  ⟨s.x, s.y, if reset = 1#1 then 0#1 else s.busy⟩
-/-- The cycle is the schedule `finish ≫ load ≫ swap ≫ subtract ≫ clear`, one rule after another. -/
-theorem next_eq_steps (reset start : BitVec 1) (a b : BitVec 8) (s : St) :
-    next reset start a b s = clear reset (subtract (swap (load start a b (finish s)))) := by
-  obtain ⟨x, y, busy⟩ := s
-  -- unfold the design's cycle
-  -- name the five rules
-  simp [next, mkGcd.design, Design.cycle, mkGcd.schedule,
-    mkGcd.interfaces, mkGcd.rules.load, mkGcd.rules.swap, mkGcd.rules.subtract,
-    mkGcd.rules.finish, mkGcd.rules.clear, mkGcd.signature, Sched.run, Action.step,
-    Action.fires, writesIf, State.write, State.cur, State.read, HList.set, HList.get,
-    Expr.eval, Expr.binVal, Expr.cmpVal, Common.putR, Common.putW, Common.memAt,
-    mkGcd.x, mkGcd.y, mkGcd.busy, mkGcd.reset, mkGcd.start, mkGcd.a, mkGcd.b] <;>
-  simp only [finish, load, swap, subtract, clear] <;>
-  bv_decide
-/-- What each rule must preserve: the gcd of the two registers. -/
-def g (s : St) : Nat := Nat.gcd s.x.toNat s.y.toNat
-theorem swap_keeps_gcd (s : St) : g (swap s) = g s := by
-  by_cases h : s.busy = 1#1 ∧ s.x < s.y ∧ s.y ≠ 0#8
-  · simp [swap, g, h, Nat.gcd_comm]
-  · simp [swap, g, h]
-theorem subtract_keeps_gcd (s : St) : g (subtract s) = g s := by
-  by_cases h : s.busy = 1#1 ∧ s.y ≤ s.x ∧ s.y ≠ 0#8
-  · have hs : subtract s = ⟨s.x - s.y, s.y, s.busy⟩ := by simp [subtract, h]
-    rw [g, hs, g]
-    simp only [BitVec.toNat_sub_of_le h.2.1]
-    exact Nat.gcd_sub_self_left (BitVec.le_def.mp h.2.1)
-  · simp [subtract, g, h]
-theorem clear_keeps_gcd (r : BitVec 1) (s : St) : g (clear r s) = g s := rfl
-/-- Each rule keeps the gcd, so the cycle keeps the gcd of whatever `load` left. -/
-theorem cycle_gcd (reset start : BitVec 1) (a b : BitVec 8) (s : St) :
-    g (next reset start a b s) = g (load start a b (finish s)) := by
-  rw [next_eq_steps]
-  simp only [clear_keeps_gcd, subtract_keeps_gcd, swap_keeps_gcd]
-/-- A busy cycle that has not finished keeps the gcd. -/
-theorem busy_cycle_keeps_gcd (reset start : BitVec 1) (a b : BitVec 8) (s : St)
-    (hb : s.busy = 1#1) (hy : s.y ≠ 0#8) : g (next reset start a b s) = g s := by
-  rw [cycle_gcd]
-  obtain ⟨x, y, busy⟩ := s
-  simp only at hb hy
-  simp [load, finish, hb, hy, g]

explain: swap and subtract both write x, so they cannot run in parallel. Their guards happen to be exclusive (x < y against x ≥ y), but ∥ requires disjoint write sets regardless of guards, so the front end rejects it. In parallel both rules would read the same old x, and a swap could not be followed by a subtraction in the same cycle.
